summary: Profiles X.509 version 3 certificates and version 2 certificate revocation lists for use on the Internet. It narrows a broad international standard to what Internet applications need. It was a proposed standard, replaced by RFC 3280.

plainLanguage.summary: An X.509 certificate says who a public key belongs to, and a certificate revocation list says which certificates have been withdrawn. This RFC narrows the X.509 formats down to a specific profile for Internet use, so that different implementations agree on what to put in a certificate and how to check one.

what is in an internet x.509 certificate

subtitle: The Internet profile of the X.509 v3 certificate and the X.509 v2 certificate revocation list.

tldr.problem: The X.509 standards define a certificate format and a revocation list format, but they leave many choices open, so implementations from different vendors could not be relied on to agree.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC profiles the X.509 v3 certificate and the X.509 v2 certificate revocation list for Internet use, names the extensions to use, and gives an algorithm for validating a certification path.
tldr.outcome: The profile gave Internet applications a common set of certificate contents and a common way to check a chain. This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 3280.

sections.title: Introduction, Requirements and the PKI Model
sections.content:
This specification is one part of a family of standards for the X.509 Public Key Infrastructure for the Internet, and it is a standalone document. It profiles the format and semantics of certificates and certificate revocation lists for the Internet PKI, describes procedures for processing certification paths in the Internet environment, provides encoding rules for popular cryptographic algorithms, and gives ASN.1 modules for the data structures defined or referenced.

The goal is to develop a profile that facilitates the use of X.509 certificates within Internet applications, for example WWW, electronic mail, user authentication and IPsec. The profile defines common representations of frequently used attributes, so that application developers can obtain the information they need without regard to the issuer of a particular certificate or CRL. It is structured around the expectations of the two kinds of people involved. Users are people and processes that use client software and are the subjects named in certificates, and the profile recognises the limitations of the platforms they use and keeps the configuration they must perform to a minimum. Administrators are the people who generally operate CAs, and their choices are deliberately limited, because unbounded choices increase the chance that a subtle administrator mistake will result in broad compromise and greatly complicate the software that has to process what the CA creates.

The model has four components. The end entity is the user of PKI certificates, or the end user system that is the subject of a certificate. The CA is the certification authority. The RA is a registration authority, an optional system to which a CA delegates certain management functions. The repository is a system, or a collection of distributed systems, that stores certificates and CRLs and serves as a means of distributing them to end entities.
sections.plainLanguage: Four kinds of system take part: the person or computer that holds a certificate, the authority that signs it, an optional authority that checks the request first, and a store that keeps the certificates and the lists of withdrawn ones. This RFC picks the parts of the X.509 formats that Internet applications need and agree on.

sections.title: Certificate Fields
sections.content:
A certificate is made of a tbsCertificate, which is the part that is signed, a signatureAlgorithm, and a signatureValue. The tbsCertificate itself has a version, a serial number, a signature, an issuer name, a validity period, a subject name, a subject public key info, optional unique identifiers, and an extensions field.

The version field describes the version of the encoded certificate: when extensions are used, as expected in this profile, version 3 is used, and if no extensions are present but a unique identifier is present, version 2 is used. Implementations SHOULD be prepared to accept any version certificate, and conforming implementations MUST recognize version 3 certificates.

The serial number is an integer assigned by the CA to each certificate, and it MUST be unique for each certificate issued by a given CA, so that the issuer name and the serial number together identify one certificate. The validity field is a sequence of two dates, notBefore and notAfter, giving the interval during which the CA warrants that it will maintain information about the status of the certificate. Dates through the year 2049 MUST be encoded as UTCTime and dates in 2050 or later MUST be encoded as GeneralizedTime, and both must be expressed in Greenwich Mean Time and must include seconds.

The subject field identifies the entity associated with the public key, and the subject name may be carried there, in the subject alternative name extension, or in both. If the subject is a CA, the subject field MUST be a non-empty distinguished name matching the issuer field in all certificates that CA issues. If the naming information is present only in the subject alternative name extension, the subject name MUST be an empty sequence and that extension MUST be critical.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate holds a serial number that the issuer must never reuse, the dates between which it is valid, the name of the person or system it belongs to, and the public key itself. All of that is signed by the issuer, along with a list of extensions.

sections.title: Certificate Extensions
sections.content:
The X.509 v3 format extends the v2 format by adding provision for additional extension fields, and particular extension field types may be specified in standards or defined and registered by any organization or community. The extension types that ISO/IEC/ITU and ANSI X9 defined are very broad in their applicability, so this document profiles them for Internet use, with a goal of interoperability for WWW, electronic mail and IPsec applications.

The standard extensions covered are the authority key identifier, the subject key identifier, key usage, the private key usage period, certificate policies, policy mappings, the subject alternative name, the issuer alternative name, subject directory attributes, basic constraints, name constraints, policy constraints, the extended key usage field and the CRL distribution points. One new Internet-specific extension is defined, the authority information access extension, which identifies the certificate's issuer and the place where the certificate can be checked for revocation, so that a relying party can find what it needs without prior arrangement.

The key usage extension states the purpose of the key in the certificate, for example encipherment, signature or certificate signing, and each permitted operation is a named bit: digital signature, non-repudiation, key encipherment, data encipherment, key agreement, certificate signing, CRL signing, and the two key agreement qualifiers. When the extension is used it SHOULD be marked critical, and the certificate signing bit may only be asserted in CA certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension field is where a certificate says the extra things an application needs: which names also belong to the key, what the key may be used for, which policies the issuer follows, and where to find the list of withdrawn certificates. This RFC picks the set that Internet applications need.

sections.title: The Certificate Revocation List
sections.content:
A certificate is expected to be in use for its entire validity period, but a change of name, the end of an employment relationship, or a compromise or suspected compromise of the corresponding private key can make a certificate invalid before it expires. X.509 defines revocation by having each CA periodically issue a signed certificate revocation list: a time-stamped list identifying revoked certificates, signed by a CA and made freely available in a public repository. Each revoked certificate is identified in the list by its serial number, and a user of a certificate checks the signature and the validity period and also acquires a suitably recent list to confirm that the serial number is not on it. The limitation of this method is that the time granularity of revocation is limited to the CRL issue period, which may be an hour, a day or a week.

The X.509 v2 CRL format is profiled for Internet use in the same way as the certificate. The signed part, the tbsCertList, carries a version, a signature, an issuer name, a thisUpdate date, a nextUpdate date, the list of revoked certificates, and any extensions. Each revoked certificate is identified by its serial number and the date of revocation, and it can carry a reason code, a hold instruction code, an invalidity date, and the name of the issuer of the revoked certificate when that differs from the issuer of the list. The CRL extensions covered are the authority key identifier, the issuer alternative name, a CRL number, a delta CRL indicator and the issuing distribution point. A delta CRL carries only the changes since the last complete CRL, and the issuing distribution point says which part of the address space a CRL covers.

The profile does not require CAs to issue CRLs at all. Message formats and protocols supporting on-line revocation notification may be defined in other PKIX specifications, and on-line checking can significantly reduce the latency between a revocation report and its reaching the parties who rely on it, at the cost of new security requirements: the certificate validator must trust the on-line validation service, whereas the repository does not need to be trusted.
sections.plainLanguage: The revocation list is a signed document from the authority listing the certificates it has withdrawn, each by serial number. This RFC defines the fields such a list carries and the extensions that let a list be split up or carry only the changes since the last one.

sections.title: Certification Path Validation
sections.content:
Certification path processing verifies the binding between the subject distinguished name or subject alternative name and the subject public key, and that binding is limited by the constraints specified in the certificates which make up the path. The basic constraints and policy constraints extensions allow the processing logic to automate the decision making. Conforming implementations are not required to implement the algorithm this document describes, but MUST be functionally equivalent to the external behaviour resulting from it.

The algorithm assumes the trusted public key is contained in a self-signed certificate, which simplifies the description; the signature on a self-signed certificate provides no security service of its own, and the key is trusted because of the other procedures used to obtain and protect it. A certification path is a sequence of n certificates where, for all x in {1, (n-1)}, the subject of certificate x is the issuer of certificate x+1, certificate 1 is the self-signed certificate, and certificate n is the end entity certificate.

The inputs are the certification path, a set of initial policy identifiers, the current date and time, and the time for which the validity of the path should be determined, which may be the current time or a point in the past. The procedure initialises five state variables: the acceptable policy set, whose initial value is the special value any-policy; the constrained subtrees, whose initial value is unbounded; the excluded subtrees, whose initial value is empty; the explicit policy variable, whose initial value is n+1 and which may be decreased but not increased; and the policy mapping variable, whose initial value is also n+1 and which may likewise be decreased but not increased. The certificates are then processed one at a time from the self-signed certificate to the end entity certificate, so that processing certificate i affects the state variables used for certificate i+1.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking a certificate means following the chain of certificates back to one the user already trusts, and at each step checking that the signatures line up, that the names are allowed, that the dates are current, and that the policies match what the application asked for. The RFC gives a step-by-step procedure, though an implementation is free to use any method that gives the same answer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The availability and freshness of revocation information affects the degree of assurance that should be placed in a certificate. While certificates expire naturally, events can occur during a certificate's natural lifetime which negate the binding between the subject and the public key, and if revocation information is untimely or unavailable the assurance associated with the binding is clearly reduced. Implementations of the path validation mechanism that omit revocation checking provide less assurance than those that support it.

The path validation algorithm depends on the certain knowledge of the public keys of one or more trusted CAs, and the decision to trust a CA is important because it determines the trust afforded a certificate. The authenticated distribution of trusted CA public keys, usually in the form of a self-signed certificate, is a security critical out of band process that is beyond the scope of this specification. Where a key compromise or CA failure occurs for a trusted CA, the user has to modify the information given to the path validation routine; selecting too many trusted CAs makes that information hard to maintain, while selecting only one may limit users to a closed community until a global PKI emerges.

The quality of implementations that process certificates also affects the degree of assurance provided, because the path validation algorithm relies on the integrity of the trusted CA information and especially of the public keys associated with the trusted CAs: by substituting a public key for which an attacker holds the private key, an attacker could trick the user into accepting false certificates. The binding between a key and a certificate subject cannot be stronger than the cryptographic module and algorithms used to generate the signature, so short key lengths or weak hash algorithms limit the utility of a certificate. Loss of a CA's private signing key is also problematic, because the CA could not then produce CRLs or perform a normal key rollover, and CAs are advised to maintain a secure backup of signing keys.
sections.plainLanguage: How much a certificate can be trusted depends on how fresh the list of withdrawn certificates is, and on the care taken with the keys of the authorities you trust. If an attacker holds the private key of a trusted authority, they can make certificates that look perfectly valid.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PKI ENTITIES IN RFC 2459

items.title: End entity
items.text: The user of PKI certificates, or the end user system that is the subject of a certificate.

items.title: Certification authority
items.text: The CA, which signs certificates and publishes certificate revocation lists.

items.title: Registration authority
items.text: An optional system to which a CA delegates certain management functions.

items.title: Repository
items.text: A system, or a collection of distributed systems, that stores certificates and CRLs and distributes them to end entities.

viz.caption: THE FIELDS OF A CERTIFICATE (RFC 2459, SECTION 4.1.2)

cells: The version of the encoded certificate, 3 when extensions are used
An integer assigned by the CA; it MUST be unique for each certificate issued by that CA
The algorithm identifier of the CA's signature over the certificate
The name of the certification authority that issued the certificate
notBefore and notAfter, the dates between which the CA warrants the certificate's status
The entity associated with the public key
The public key and its algorithm identifier
Additional fields, each marked critical or non-critical

items.label: Digital signature
items.desc: The key verifies digital signatures other than certificate or CRL signatures.

items.label: Non-repudiation
items.desc: The key verifies signatures that protect against the signer falsely denying an action.

items.label: Key encipherment
items.desc: The key is used for key transport.

items.label: Data encipherment
items.desc: The key enciphers user data, other than cryptographic keys.

items.label: Key agreement
items.desc: The key is used for key agreement.

items.label: Certificate signing
items.desc: The key verifies a signature on certificates. It may only be asserted in CA certificates.

items.label: CRL signing
items.desc: The key verifies a signature on revocation information.
